What is the equation of the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram we see that the arms of the parabola open to the right. The parabola has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(2,-2).$

The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(0,0)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(2,-2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=-2$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ (-2)^{2} & =4p(2) \\ 4 & =8p \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(\frac{1}{2})x \\ {y}^{2} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the arms of the parabola open to the right since $p=\frac{1}{2}$ is positive.

\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x+4) \\ (2+3)^{2} & =4p(1+4) \\ 25 & =20p \\ p & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x+4) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =4(\frac{5}{4})(x+4) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =5(x+4).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(1,-3)$ and passes through the point $(3,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(h,k)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,-3),$ we substitute $h=1$ and $k=-3$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(3,0),$ so we can substitute $x=3$ and $y=0$ into the equation above and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1) \\ (0+3)^{2} & =4p(3-1) \\ 9 & =8p \\ p & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =4(\frac{9}{8})(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{9}{2}(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$
